frameworks.name: Time Study Measurement System
frameworks.definition: A 15-minute interval time-tracking system using a kitchen timer and single-sheet logging to identify how a founder allocates their week and expose high-ROI delegation opportunities.

frameworks.name: Founder-to-Owner Transition Model
frameworks.definition: A conceptual framework where an entrepreneur systematically hires replacements for each time allocation, converting from founder-dependent service delivery to owner-level profit distribution.

frameworks.name: Unicorn Decomposition Strategy
frameworks.definition: Rejecting the search for a single all-capable hire (the "unicorn") and instead partitioning the founder's role into discrete sub-roles (white horse + rhino horn + fireflies) that can be hired separately and executed in parallel.

claims.text: Time auditing for one week using 15-minute interval logging will immediately expose the founder's least-efficient time allocations, creating awareness that shifts behavior toward delegation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Visible allocation data breaks through founder rationalization and reveals objective misalignment between personal capacity and business needs.
bounded_by: Does not address which activities to delegate, only reveals them

claims.text: Approximately 40% of a founder's weekly time is typically spent on a single repetitive function that can be fully staffed as a role, and the time-recovery ROI (doubling business value) exceeds the cost of the hire.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Time recapture enables founder to compound business growth at higher leverage than the hire's salary cost.
bounded_by: Does not apply to founder-magic-dependent businesses where personal touch is the product

claims.text: Entrepreneurs are fundamentally "many-headed fractionalists" who pull activities onto their plate until there is enough volume to justify a full-time role, then ship it to someone else.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Founder adds scope until a discrete function reaches 1.0 FTE equivalent, making delegation a natural transition rather than premature hire.

claims.text: The entire process of entrepreneurship is trading up: converting current time allocation into higher-unit compensation (dollars per hour), repeatedly, until the business operates without founder time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each delegation cycle frees founder bandwidth to apply to higher-leverage activities, compounding the business value relative to time spent.
bounded_by: Does not prescribe a final exit; the trade-up cycle continues indefinitely

claims.text: A fully operational business where the founder can hire someone to replicate their role entirely generates owner-level distributions after the hire's salary is deducted from profit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder no longer required for daily delivery
claims.mechanism: Transferring execution authority to a hire separates ownership economics (profit distribution) from labor economics (salary), enabling owner to extract passive return.
bounded_by: Assumes operations are sufficiently systematized to be handed off

claims.text: When a founder claims 'no one can do what I do,' they are correct, but the claim reveals incomplete delegation strategy: instead of hiring a single replacement, the founder should partition their role into 2-3 specialized sub-roles that collectively execute better than the founder alone.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business has matured to require delegation
claims.mechanism: Specialization and full-time focus by 2-3 people exceeds generalist founder performance across all dimensions because each hire dedicates their full time to one function rather than the founder splitting attention.
bounded_by: Assumes the founder's role is composite (sales + delivery + systems) rather than a singular unique skill

claims.text: The founder's core resource is time; optimal time allocation is the single lever that determines business leverage and the founder's earned income multiplier.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Explicit time valuation (hourly rate required vs. available) creates a decision filter for delegation: any task below the founder's threshold rate is delegable.

claims.text: Mission-driven entrepreneurs continue the founder-role partitioning cycle even after achieving owner status, stacking their plate with higher-leverage activities (strategy, vision, new products) instead of taking passive distributions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder psychology: ambition-driven rather than income-driven
claims.mechanism: Reinvesting freed time into new initiatives compounds business growth and founder wealth more than extraction would.
bounded_by: Does not apply to founders optimizing for lifestyle or work-life balance

examples.text: A founder audits their time weekly using 15-minute intervals and discovers 40% of their effort goes to customer support. By hiring one person full-time to handle all support, the founder frees 20 hours per week. If the business can double revenue with 20 founder hours per week of sales focus, and the hire costs less than the business growth delta, the economic trade is positive. The founder was previously unaware of this opportunity until time was made visible.

A founder operates as the salesperson, delivery manager, and operator. They cannot be replaced by one hire because no single person has all three capabilities. However, hiring a dedicated salesperson, a project manager, and an operations coordinator—three people total—allows each to focus their full time on one function. These three collectively deliver better results than the founder alone because none are context-switching between roles.

practices.text: Conduct a time-study audit for one week: create a Google Sheet with 15-minute time slots from 5 a.m. to midnight, set a kitchen timer for each interval, and when it rings, log one to two words describing what you just did. Do not skip this even if it feels inefficient—this week will be the most productive of your life because awareness drives behavior change.

After completing the time audit, identify the single largest time sink (typically ~40% of the week). Calculate the cost to hire a person to do that function full-time, then compare that cost to the business value you could generate if you got those hours back. If the business multiplier exceeds the hire cost, proceed immediately to delegation and hiring.

For each subsequent 15% time block identified in your audit, ask three questions in sequence: (1) Can I hire someone to do this full-time? (2) Can I systematize or push this responsibility down to an existing team member? (3) If neither is viable yet, how much more of this function do I need to accumulate before it justifies a full-time role? Continue until the answer to (1) becomes yes.

When facing the belief that no one can replace you, reframe the problem as finding 2-3 specialized people (white horse + horn + fireflies) instead of one unicorn. Partition your role into discrete functions, describe what 100% success looks like for each, and hire for those discrete outcomes rather than searching for a generalist replacement.
